evidence: Officers of color land with Leclerc (Pétion, Rigaud). The 1792 equality law is in force. Napoleon’s secret instructions (October 31, 1801) plan deportation of leaders, but they are not public.
Toussaint submits; officers of color still command. The law of May 20, 1802 keeps slavery in the colonies that never applied abolition.

In Guadeloupe, Richepanse restores slavery and reserves the title of citizen for whites (July 16–17), repealing the 1792 equality law there. A July 2 decree bars people of color from entering France. Disarmament breeds the “greatest discontent.”
sources: Richepanse <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_Richepanse>; Decree of 29 March 1815 (history of the 1802 decrees) <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decree_of_29_March_1815>

evidence: Pétion and Clervaux leave French service (October 13–14). Leclerc disarms about 1,200 native soldiers; Black and mulatto prisoners are drowned at Le Cap. Leclerc’s orders call for deporting leading officers of color.
